        EREN: Mapping the Central Administration in the Later Roman Empire: The Epigraphic Representation and Elite Networks of the Palatine Bureaucracy

        Before the European Union, the late Roman Empire was the first uniform, hierarchically structured system of the pre-modern world, with infrastructure across most of Europe and the Mediterranean grounded in an overarching institutional, legal and cultural framework. This extraordinary phenomenon of central supra-regional institutions and networks of governing elites has rarely been scrutinized in scholarly accounts from an epigraphic and digital humanities perspective.

        As MSCA Fellow, Dr. Mariana Bodnaruk will receive crucial training in digital humanities and mixed-methods approaches at the University of Warsaw and study the late Roman state’s elaborate centralized machine, whose officials, with their high political mobility, were set apart from other social strata as bureaucrats in the imperial service. The aim is to investigate what generated empire-wide mobility networks of Roman elites, and how, despite regional differences, officials were able to construct and sustain a supra-regional institutional framework. Dr. Bodnaruk will collect data in an online database and construct a digital map to visualize elite networks. A three-month secondment at the Austrian Academy of Sciences will help them extend their training and research.

        What were the diachronic transformations of spatial and social representation and networks of Roman palatine functionaries?

        The project's research question

        The overarching research objectives are to conduct a comprehensive empirical inquiry into court office-holders across the fourth-century empire, to study epigraphic data by applying a novel methodology informed by the digital and material turn, and to compare the urban epigraphic representation of state bureaucrats and their networks in wider socio-political and cultural contexts, answering the research question: What were the diachronic transformations of spatial and social representation and networks of Roman palatine functionaries?

        Dr. Bodnaruk will produce groundbreaking mixed-methods research beyond the state of the art in Roman epigraphy, history and digital humanities; an online database and map; outreach and dissemination to crucial target audiences; and publications on new methods in epigraphy.

        News

        3 entries · 2025–2026

        1. 26 March 2026

          From 24 to 26 March 2026, Mariana participated in an EpiDoc training in Graz.

          The training was organized as part of the tenth Epigraphy.info workshop. EpiDoc is a leading TEI XML standard for editing ancient Latin and Greek inscriptions. Gaining EpiDoc skills significantly increases Mariana’s ability to seek employment and design new editorial projects.

          The post on the current EREN website
        2. 1 March 2026

          The international conference Inscribed Art in the Late Roman West and Early Medieval Mediterranean Worlds (ca. 284–800 CE) will take place on 15–16 May 2026 at the Faculty of History, University of Warsaw.

          The conference is organized by Dr. Mariana Bodnaruk (Faculty of History, University of Warsaw).

          The conference will focus on inscribed art of Late Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages, examining the relationship between image, text, and material object. Papers may address inscriptions on monuments, mosaics, frescoes, coins, seals, ceramics, and everyday objects, and explore their role in shaping political authority, religious practices, social identities, and daily life. The thematic and geographical scope includes the late Roman Empire as well as the Mediterranean, the Caucasus, the Near East, and parts of Africa.

          The organizers invite proposals for 20-minute papers in English. The conference will be held in person, participation is free of charge, and the conference proceedings will be published as an edited volume.

          Applications are welcome from scholars at all career stages, with particular encouragement for early-career researchers.

          Submission deadline

        3. 1 September 2025

          Today we warmly welcome Dr. Mariana Bodnaruk as a new researcher at the Faculty of History, University of Warsaw!

          Dr. Mariana Bodnaruk has been awarded a “Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Postdoctoral Fellowship” to carry out the project “Mapping the central administration in the late Roman Empire: epigraphic imagery and networks of the palace bureaucracy’s elite”.

          The supervisor of the postdoctoral fellowship is Dr. Paweł Nowakowski, who hopes that the research will contribute to the development of epigraphic studies, much of which he is carrying out within the ERC-funded STONE-MASTERS project.

          Dr. Bodnaruk intends to investigate the mobility of elites in the Late Roman Empire. They seek to answer the question of how the elites of the late Roman Empire built and maintained institutions that held together a multitude of peoples and cultures – a structure in which certain parallels can be drawn with the European Union, which emerged many centuries later, despite obvious and sometimes drastic differences.

          Their project also aims to answer the question of what led to the emergence of a network of bureaucratic mobility and how – despite regional differences – officials were able to build and maintain a supra-regional institutional framework.

          Dr. Mariana Bodnaruk will draw on the principles and achievements of digital humanities. Among other things, they plan to create a digital catalogue to disseminate knowledge about the Empire’s elite networks.

        This international conference will explore inscribed art of the late Roman Empire and the Mediterranean from the late third to the late eighth century CE. Focusing on the intersection of image, text, and object, it examines inscriptions on monuments, mosaics and frescoes, seals and coins, vessels, ceramics, and other serialized items, including both display and utilitarian pieces.

        Prosopography

        In preparation

        Prosopographical table

        This section of the website will contain a link to a prosopographical table, which is currently being prepared within the project.

        While epigraphic databases are currently available, no database of late Roman court members exists, and no attempts at visualization have been made on the basis of existing materials. Inscriptions pertaining to praetorian prefects in the regional administration from 284 to 395 have, however, recently been presented as a searchable database (PPRET). The epigraphic record of the imperial elite can therefore boast a high-quality digital edition of previously known and currently available inscriptions, which can subsequently be increased by publications of more recent finds.

        There is a need for a digital epigraphic corpus of the bureaucrats in the central administration that would incorporate both inscriptions scattered in the printed corpora and considerable more recent additions dispersed in journal publications, as well as work in progress on new finds from ongoing archaeological missions. Dr. Bodnaruk will construct an open catalogue of the court officials, which will facilitate analyses of their urban and social representation. This research question requires an update of the epigraphic sources pertaining to the court members and a re-reading of the legal, literary and papyrological evidence essential for the analysis of the palatine bureaucrats as social actors forming elite networks.

        Team

        Faculty of History, University of Warsaw

        Mariana Bodnaruk

        Principal investigator · MSCA Fellow

        Dr. Mariana Bodnaruk is Assistant Professor in Ancient History at the Faculty of History of the University of Warsaw. They received a PhD in Medieval Studies from Central European University in Budapest (2019).

        They have taught at Al-Quds Bard College, Central European University, Bard College, Masaryk University, and the University of Olomouc. Their research has been published in the Journal of Epigraphic Studies, the Journal of Late Antiquity, Antichthon, and Phoenix. They were a Postdoctoral Fellow at the Department of Art History and Archaeology of the University of Fribourg in 2021 and 2022–24.

        They authored An Empire of Elites: The Self-Representation of the Senatorial Aristocracy in the Later Roman State in the Fourth Century AD and edited Artistic Practice, Materiality and Ideology in the Medieval East Roman Empire and Neighboring Eastern Polities. Their research interests include epigraphy, art history, and hagiography of the medieval East Roman Empire, queer and trans studies, and historical materialism.

        m.bodnaruk@uw.edu.plUniversity profile

        Paweł Nowakowski

        Advisor

        Dr. Paweł Nowakowski is the advisor appointed to oversee the MSCA training of Dr. Mariana Bodnaruk.

        He is a historian and epigraphist of the late antique period. Since 2018, he has held a lectureship in ancient history at the Department of Ancient History of the Faculty of History, University of Warsaw – first as an assistant, and since 2019 as an assistant professor. Since 2022, he has been running the ERC-funded project STONE-MASTERS (Starting Grant 101040152).
